title: Higher-codimension residue transitions
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $T$ a Noetherian excellent scheme with $\ell$ invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Use costalks $C_{\bar t}M=R\Gamma_{\bar t}M$, roots-of-unity twists, and normalized immediate residue transitions as specified in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. A geometric specialization $\bar u\rightsquigarrow\bar v$ is a map of strict localizations over $T$ [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]; its codimension $c$ is the dimension of the reduced closure of its general point in the strict localization at its special point. For every $M\in D^+(T_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ and $a\in\mathbf Z$ there is a natural transition
$$\operatorname{sp}_{\bar u,\bar v}:H^a(C_{\bar u}M)\longrightarrow H^{a+2c}(C_{\bar v}M(c)).$$
For $c=1$ it is the normalized residue transition of the cited definition; for $c=0$ it is the transport for the specified geometric specialization. These maps are compatible with composition: for composable geometric specializations of codimensions $c,d$, the composite transition, with its intervening twist and degree shift, is the transition for their composite, of codimension $c+d$. In particular they give the same composite along two sides of any commutative square of geometric specializations. A specialization can be factored into a finite chain of immediate specializations (and a codimension-zero transport), and its transition is independent of the chosen factorization.

source.place: Expose XVII, Theorem 3.1.2 and section 3.5 (general transitions, naturality, transitivity and independence of factorization); geometric codimension and immediate specializations as in XIV section 2.1.

proof.text: For positive codimension use the canonical transition maps of [lem-per-normal-top-residue-class], with $X=T$. Its coefficient ring is exactly $\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, its complex is an arbitrary bounded-below etale complex, and its maps are natural in that complex. Its codimension-one agreement is with the normalization of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex], so taking cohomology gives the required immediate maps. In codimension zero define the map by transport of the geometric fibre of $R\Gamma_t M$ along the specified geometric specialization. This is a map of complexes before taking cohomology: a codimension-zero specialization is a morphism in the Galois groupoid of the residue field. On representatives of the geometric-fibre colimit it transports the pointed neighbourhood and keeps its section. It is the identity for the identity specialization and is functorial in $M$. No assertion that a nonidentity Galois transport acts trivially is used.

source.place: XVII, Theorem 3.1.2; Definition 1.1.1, Definition 1.4.1 and Remark 1.4.2 (printed pp. 258–263, 268)

proof.text: Let $\alpha:\bar u\rightsquigarrow\bar v$ and $\beta:\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar w$ have codimensions $c,d$. Apply the composition clause of [lem-per-normal-top-residue-class]. With twists and degrees written out it says that the map for $\beta\alpha$ is the composite of $H^a(C_{\bar u}M)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{sp}_{\alpha}}H^{a+2c}(C_{\bar v}M(c))$ and $H^{a+2c}(C_{\bar v}M(c))\xrightarrow{\operatorname{sp}_{\beta}}H^{a+2c+2d}(C_{\bar w}M(c)(d))$. Identify $M(c)(d)$ with $M(c+d)$ using the signed twists of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. This gives the claimed degree $a+2(c+d)$ and twist $c+d$. When a codimension is zero, use the same node’s compatibility with strict-local restriction: changing the specified geometric fibre by that strict-local isomorphism conjugates the positive-codimension map by its transport. Thus the same formula holds with the transport defined in Step 1. If both codimensions vanish, transporting a representative section twice equals transport along the composite map of pointed neighbourhoods. This verifies the formula also for two nontrivial Galois transports.

In a commutative square let the two paths from the initial geometric point to the final one be $\beta\alpha$ and $\delta\gamma$. They are the same specified geometric specialization, not just the same pair of underlying Zariski points. Step 2 identifies both composites of transition maps with the transition for that specialization, with the same total degree and twist. Hence the two composites agree.

Apply only the geometric assertion in [lem-per-general-costalk-transitions]: every positive-codimension geometric specialization has a finite immediate factorization. This assertion is about $T$ and the specified geometric specialization, with no coefficient-dependent object in its conclusion. Its hypotheses hold for our $T$ and prime $\ell$; if a complex is required, instantiate that theorem with the zero $\mathbf F_\ell$-complex. We take no $\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$ cohomology map from this prime-field theorem. Retain any codimension-zero transport needed to realize the specified geometric arrow, rather than merely a Zariski chain. For a codimension-zero arrow, that arrow itself is the required transport and the immediate chain is empty.

For a factorization $\alpha_r\cdots\alpha_1$, use induction on $r$ to compare its transition composite with the transition of the specified arrow. For $r=0$ this is the identity transport. For $r=1$ it is Step 1. If the assertion holds for $r-1$, Step 2 applied to $\alpha_r$ and $\alpha_{r-1}\cdots\alpha_1$ proves it for $r$; the degrees and twists add by integer addition. Thus every factorization from Step 4 gives the same transition. In particular two choices of intermediate geometric points or chains produce equal maps whenever their geometric composites equal the specified specialization.

proof_origin.place: XVII, Theorem 3.1.2, Remark 1.4.2 and Sections 3.5.1–3.5.2; reusing the pre-existing general-transition and geometric-factorization nodes

Statement unchanged; no new nodes; no SGA; live item still unsplit, so not superseded. Step 1: cites the first paragraph of lem-per-normal-top-residue-class, which needs no normality and matches the item's hypotheses: Z/ℓ^n, Noetherian excellent X, all of D+, natural maps, c=1 normalization from def-per-potential-dualizing-complex. The c=0 Galois transport is defined directly, per ILO 1.4.2. Step 2: checked degrees and twists (a→a+2c→a+2(c+d), M(c)(d)≅M(c+d) via signed twists); mixed c=0 cases use the strict-local restriction compatibility. Step 3 (square) and Step 5 (induction r=0, r=1, successor) are elementary. Step 4 uses only the geometric finite-factorization sentence of lem-per-general-costalk-transitions with M=0, so no F_ℓ to Z/ℓ^n identification is needed; independently, excellent ⇒ catenary gives chains of length c. Edge cases checked: nontrivial Galois at c=0, c=d=0, identity arrow, n=1. Proof closure (2232 nodes) contains no cycle. (2) That node's wording 'identity when c=0' should read 'evident transport isomorphism (ILO 1.4.2)'; literally it is false for nontrivial Galois elements.
